title: The rule at work
hookLine: which parts of your rule travel to work? Abba Hilkiah keeps hoeing, and Baizhang won't eat on a day without work
tomorrow: in Genesis, what came before the very first job?

lines: A DROUGHT, AND A MAN WHO PRAYS.
cards: Monday morning, the laptop opening, and the long sit you planned feels like something from another life. The Talmud tells of a drought, and of a man named Abba Hilkiah whose prayers, people said, brought rain.
The rabbis sent two scholars to ask him to pray. They found him hoeing in a field. They greeted him.
He didn't answer, and he didn't look up.

teach.b: He worked to the end of the day and walked home. Only then did he and his wife go up to the roof to pray, and the clouds came. Afterward the scholars asked why he hadn't returned their greeting.
His answer, in substance: I was hired by the day, and I wouldn't take my employer's time.
That small story carries a real Jewish teaching: a worker's hours belong to the one who pays for them, and Jewish law makes room for prayer inside those hours.

teach.h: THE SHEMA AT THE TOP OF A TREE.
teach.b: The Mishnah says craftsmen may recite the Shema right where they are, at the top of a tree or on a course of stones, without climbing down. The prayer comes to the job, in a form that fits it.
So, today's question: which parts of a rule travel to work?
This tradition's answer: the parts that fit inside honest work without stealing from it. Now a neighbor. The Chan master Baizhang, tradition says, kept working in the monastery fields into old age.
When his monks hid his tools so he would rest, he wouldn't eat that day: a day without work, a day without food. What's shared: both hold honest work as part of a holy life.
The honest difference: Baizhang's monks made the work itself the practice, while the Mishnah keeps prayer and paid work distinct, and fits the prayer around hours that belong to someone else.

how: The Mishnah allows workers to recite the Shema where they are working, and Jewish law treats an employer's hours as owed; in Chan monasteries, work in the fields was part of the monks' practice. On a personal rule, one short part is chosen to travel to work.

games.q: what does “the rule at work” mean?
o: a list of rules your employer sets for the office
doing all of your practice during work hours
the parts of your rule that travel with you to your job

games.q: a prayer in the treetop: tap the pairs.
p: kept hoeing; the day was his employer's
the Shema at the top of a tree
a day without work, a day without food
work as practice, or prayer fitted to work

s: Abba Hilkiah ignored the rabbis out of pride
he was hired by the day and wouldn't take his employer's time.
the Mishnah lets craftsmen recite the Shema at the top of a tree
the prayer comes to the work, without climbing down.
a spiritual practice should always come before your job's hours
in this teaching, honest work has its own claim, and the practice fits around it.

games.q: a nurse wants to keep her midday prayer, but her shift is packed. by the Mishnah's way, what fits?
o: a short form she can say at her station without leaving her patients.
leave the ward for a long prayer; practice comes before the job.
drop prayer on workdays; work and faith don't mix.
games.why: the Mishnah lets craftsmen say the Shema at the top of a tree. the prayer goes to the work, in a form that fits it.

practice: Sit the way you sit at your desk, hands where the keyboard would be. Go through your rule part by part and ask whether it fits inside your work hours without stealing from them.
Pick one part that does, and rest with it as the part that travels.

wordCard.voice: The rule at work: the parts of your rule that travel to your job, fitted inside honest work. Abba Hilkiah prayed after the hoeing.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear, the first word of the Shema, which the Mishnah lets workers say on the job.

carryVoice: For Monday: at work, the part that fits without stealing anyone's time. Day 1707, and the rule goes out the door.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a-b (Abba Hilkiah hoeing in the field; does not return the scholars' greeting; prays with his wife on the roof; hired by the day, he would not interrupt his work)
Mishnah Berakhot 2:4 (craftsmen may recite the Shema at the top of a tree or on a course of stones)
Baizhang Huaihai, as told in the Chan records (Transmission of the Lamp): the hidden tools; 'a day without work, a day without food'
